messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh Nguyen is a 44-year-old nurse who works the night shift at a community hospital in San Jose. He has been married to his wife, Linh, for sixteen years. Eight months ago, after a long double shift, he walked toward his car in the hospital's dimly lit parking garage around three in the morning. A man came up from behind, pressed something hard against his ribs, and demanded his wallet. Minh handed it over, but the man shoved him anyway, hard enough that Minh's head struck the concrete pillar beside him. The man grabbed the wallet and ran. Minh lay on the ground for several minutes, dazed, tasting blood from where his cheek had split. He had a small fracture in his jaw that healed in six weeks. But the memory did not heal.

What stayed with him, what returned again and again, was not the story of the event but the exact, still images he could summon at will—the grain of the concrete pillar under his cheek, the pattern of the man's sneakers as he ran away, the angle of the fluorescent light bars above him. The memories came as photographs, silent and sharp, and when they arrived he felt a sharp ache along his left jaw and a pressure in his ribs, precisely where the man had pushed and where his head had struck. He had come to believe that there must be something about him—the way he carried himself, the way he had walked too slowly, some inherent carelessness—that had made the man choose him. That thought burrowed into him over the weeks that followed. Nothing good can happen to me anymore, he started telling himself, and then, later, more quietly, I have no future.

Minh stopped leaving the hospital after dark if he could help it, but he could not change his shift entirely. On the nights he did walk out, he scanned the garage from the moment he pressed the elevator button, rotating his head constantly, checking blind corners, turning to glance behind him every few steps. He began to sit in his car for ten minutes before driving, watching the rearview mirror for anyone approaching. That mirror-checking spread into other parts of his life: at home, he caught himself looking at the bathroom mirror to see if someone was behind him; at the grocery store, he stole glances at the convex security mirrors in the aisles. In the hospital itself, during his breaks in the staff lounge, he always chose a seat against the wall, one where he could see the door and the window at the same time, even if it meant sitting away from his colleagues. If someone sat behind him, he could not focus on his food.

The consequences accumulated quietly. Linh noticed that he no longer accepted invitations to join friends for dinner at restaurants, because he would spend the whole evening checking the entrance and the windows. He told her he was tired, and he was—falling asleep had become a struggle, and staying asleep was worse. He would jolt awake at two or three in the morning, convinced he had heard footsteps on the driveway, and would lie in the dark, staring at the bedroom door. He started to keep his mind occupied all the time: podcasts during his commute, music at home, the television on low all night. Silence left room for the images.

What finally brought Minh to seek help was a shift in the emergency department two weeks ago. A patient was brought in after a street assault, and as Minh helped clean the man's facial lacerations, the still images of his own injury—the concrete, the fluorescent lights—flashed so vividly that he had to excuse himself and sit in the staff bathroom for fifteen minutes, pressing his fingers against his jaw. Later that night, he realized that he could not remember the last time he had looked forward to anything. He called a clinic the next morning. He is afraid that if he lets himself feel the fear fully, he will fall apart completely, and he is equally afraid that nothing will change. But he comes because Linh has started to sleep in the guest room, and because the day before he called, he had driven past a construction site with a half-lit parking lot and had felt the same cold certainty that he had no future at all.
